title: Bhai Jaita becomes Jivan Singh
hookLine: the man who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head was embraced by the tenth Guru, who called his people the Guru's own sons

lines: ONE MAN MOVES TOWARD THE BODY.
cards: Delhi, in the square of Chandni Chowk. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, has just been executed on the emperor's order. His body lies where it fell, with guards around it, as a warning.
Sikhs in the crowd are afraid even to be recognized. Then night comes, and with it, in the story, a storm and confusion. And one man moves toward the Guru's body when everyone else is moving away.
He is a Sikh named Jaita. Today: Bhai Jaita becomes Jivan Singh.

teach.h: HE CARRIED THE HEAD TO ANANDPUR.
teach.b: Tradition says Bhai Jaita took the Guru's head, wrapped it, and carried it away from Delhi, traveling hard and in secret, all the way to Kiratpur and Anandpur, to the Guru's young son, Gobind Rai.

Others took care of the body, and a Sikh named Lakhi Shah burned his own house to cremate it unseen. But it was Jaita who arrived before the boy with his father's head. Here is the moment Sikhs remember.
Jaita came from a community that the society around him counted low. The young Guru did not see that.
Tradition says he embraced Jaita and said words Sikhs still repeat: Rangrete Guru ke bete. The Rangretas are the Guru's own sons. Not servants.

Not followers allowed in at the edge. Sons. A whole people, looked down on by the society around them, named family in one sentence, because one of them had walked toward the Guru's body when others walked away.
Years later, when the Khalsa was formed, tradition says Jaita took amrit and received a new name: Jivan Singh. Jivan means life.
He became a commander and a poet in the Guru's service, and tradition says he fell at Chamkaur. So his story carries two names. Jaita, the man who carried a head through the night.

Jivan Singh, the man the Khalsa made. Between them is the embrace: a boy whose father had just been killed, holding the man who brought him home, and making sure everyone heard what the Guru thought of him.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Jaita, later Bhai Jivan Singh, at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi and at Anandpur, and the young Guru's words 'Rangrete Guru ke bete' are repeated as a sign that the Guru made the overlooked his own family.

practice: Bring to mind someone the people around you tend to look past: the worker nobody greets by name, the relative who always gets talked over.
The young Guru didn't answer Jaita with a private kind thought; he called him family where everyone could hear.
Picture what it would look like to treat this person as one of yours, openly, with a greeting by name or a seat beside you.

wordCard.voice: Jivan Singh. The name Bhai Jaita received in the Khalsa, after carrying Guru Tegh Bahadur's head to Anandpur and being embraced as the Guru's own son. Today's word.
